Crash Course Philosophy is brought to you
by Squarespace. Squarespace: share your passion with the world. Remember when you were little and your mom told you to eat your spinach so you’d grow up big and strong? Or in college, when you set your clock ten minutes ahead, to fool yourself into getting to class on time? We all engage in useful fictions – things that we choose to believe, because, they just make life easier. And when we do this, we are being pragmatists. Pragmatism is based on the theory that finding
true beliefs is less important than finding beliefs that work,
practically, in the living of your life. In this view, it doesn’t really matter whether
spinach actually helps muscle growth; if eating spinach will improve your life, and believing that it’ll make you strong convinces you to eat it – then it’s a useful belief, which is
all that matters. Pragmatism is relatively recent as philosophical
movements go. But some of the most well-known American pragmatists – like William James, and, I would argue,
Indiana Jones – have an ideological ancestor in 17th century
mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal. You can be a pragmatist about basically anything – knowledge, spinach, metaphysics, ethics,
or whether it’s actually 11:30 right now or 11:40. But Pascal took a pragmatic approach to one of the biggest issues in philosophy: God’s existence. [Theme Music] Pascal was a theist, which, given his place
in history may not be all that surprising. But what is weird is that Pascal’s argument for God’s existence had very little to do with whether God was actually real. Instead, it had everything to do with with
whether belief in his existence was practical. This reasoning became known as Pascal’s Wager, and it’s really a gambler’s argument for religious belief. Pascal’s thinking went like this: Either God exists or he doesn’t, and reason
will never give us an answer. So you must choose blindly to believe or not to
believe in God – you can’t abstain from choosing If you choose to believe in God and he exists,
you get an infinite reward – heaven. If you choose to believe in God and he doesn’t
exist, you’re not really out much. If you choose not to believe in God and he
doesn’t exist, you also don’t gain much. If you choose not to believe in God and he
does exist, you get infinite punishment – hell. Therefore, the smart bet is to put your
chips on God existing, every time. Pascal argued that, if there is the slightest chance that God exists – even if that chance is low – only a fool would bet against his existence,
given that the stakes are so high. In the face of incomplete information, Pascal
decided, we should play the odds, and believe whatever
offers us the greatest benefit. It’s kind of brilliant, right? But there are a couple of ways you could argue
against this. You might say Pascal’s done the math wrong
– that choosing to walk the straight and narrow in the service of an imaginary deity
actually does cost you something. Like, you might miss out on stuff that you
would otherwise want to do – like, sleeping in on Sunday mornings, or living a heavy-metal-rock-star lifestyle, or, I dunno, coveting stuff. By this logic, you’d lose out if you abstained
from all of that in the name of something that ended up not being real. But Pascal, like William James, disagreed
with this line of reasoning, because he saw great personal benefit in being
a believer. He thought theists have better lives, not because God is blessing them as some kind of reward, but because belief simply has inherent benefits – like the security of feeling that the world
is ordered and meaningful… That someone is always looking out for you… That death isn’t the end. Now, even if you agree that religious belief is comforting, you might still question Pascal’s motives. Does believing in something because it’s
the safest bet really win you a ticket to heaven? Doesn’t God want you to be less self-interested
when it comes to believing in him? Well, not according to Pascal. He thought how and why you choose to believe
doesn’t really matter, because the fact is, God doesn’t care how he gets you, as long
as he gets you. OK, so how do you will yourself into believing in something, just because it’s where the smart money is? Easy! Pascal said you essentially brainwash
yourself into true belief, so that what starts out as self-interest can
eventually grow into an honest conviction. And you do this, basically, by walking the
walk and talking the talk. Start going to church. Start praying.
Hang out with other believers. At first it might seem weird and disingenuous, but over time, it’ll become an ingrained part of your belief system. You know what it’s kind of like?
Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade. It’s probably pop-culture’s finest allegory
of pragmatic belief in action. Throughout the whole Indiana Jones trilogy – I’m just gonna pretend the fourth one was never made – Indy is painted as a pretty agnostic character. He hunts religious relics for a living, but the powers that those relics are said
to possess are just “hocus pocus” to him. So, at the end of The Last Crusade,
(spoilers) Indy manages to find the Holy Grail, in an ancient temple, after getting through
a bunch of booby traps. And each trap is kind of a test of faith. He has to know where to kneel, and how to
spell the name of God, and he has to jump into an abyss with the
hope that he will somehow survive. Indy ends up passing all of these tests. But not because he suddenly stops being agnostic and starts believing in God – at least not that we know of. Instead, he just does what he has to do.
He’s literally going through the motions. There’s something about that, that would
make Pascal proud. Because, to him, it would probably look like Indy was on the path to eventually, truly believing. Now, some critics have pointed out that, when
it comes to a really usable belief system, you’re gonna need morethan just: fake it
‘til you make it. For example, maybe you were one of those kids, raised in a religious household, who was just never feeling it. We all know people who were immersed in a
culture of religious belief from birth, but end up to rejecting those beliefs as adults.

Philosophy's core concept: practicality 


**What is Pragmatism?**

Pragmatism emphasizes usefulness. It focuses on finding beliefs that directly improve daily life rather than purely on adhering to beliefs deemed true. In essence, believing what leads to a more positive life experience is the key for practical belief systems. This notion was prominent among American pragmatists like William James and Indiana Jones but has roots in 17th-century mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal's thought.

**Pascal's Wager:**

Philosopher Pascal explored this pragmatism idea through a wager on God's existence: belief serves as a beneficial bet, regardless of any real proof. In Pascal's reasoning, if there is an even slight chance that God exists, choosing faith in his existence offers infinite reward – heaven. If someone chooses to believe but God doesn’t exist, the potential punishment might be nonexistent and relatively negligible. Conversely, not believing might only bring about a loss on some less vital scales. 

**Pascal's Logic and its Critics:**

This reasoning became known as Pascal’s Wager. It proposes that when facing uncertainty, one should bet on the existence of God, considering the highest value as his reward even after considering that he might not exist or there are no real repercussions if they don't exist. 

While some argue about Pascal’s perspective, William James, like Pascal, believed in the positive benefits of faith on individuals, not just its perceived rewards or punishments. According to Pascal and James, a belief leads to a sense of order, meaning, and security from death.

**How Pascal Proposed "Pragmatic Belief":**

For Pascal, finding solace and purpose can inspire someone to fully embrace a belief system through the process (walking the walk by believing in God and engaging with other believers).  He believes this is a self-imposed “brainwash.” This leads individuals toward an honest conviction which develops over time. For example, attending Church, praying, or connecting with fellow believers could potentially strengthen and deepen individual’s religious life.

**The 'Indy' Paradigm: Pragmatic Belief in Action**:
 
 Pascal might have found inspiration for his theory when viewing the Indiana Jones movie franchise. The story follows Indiana Jones who, throughout his adventurous pursuits, often encounters spiritual tests and challenges within ancient ruins. The films show Indiana overcoming obstacles by taking a practical approach – doing whatever is necessary to succeed and find what he seeks – not necessarily based on faith's religious beliefs or expectations. 

**Criticisms of Pascal’s ViewPoint:**

Some have also challenged the pragmatic viewpoint, arguing for genuine belief's essence as a matter of personal transformation beyond just "faking it" until real belief occurs. The challenge is in creating a self-sufficient foundation rather than simply relying on external pressures or rituals to foster genuine conviction and faith. 


This approach to philosophy highlights that believing for its sake doesn't guarantee true spiritual fulfillment, but adopting a practical perspective with constant evaluation might facilitate deeper understanding and more impactful convictions over time.

This transcript discusses Pascal's "Wager," a philosophical argument for religious belief developed by Blaise Pascal based on pragmatic considerations. 

**Pascal's Wager:**
* The Wager proposed that individuals choose to believe in God or not, relying on an assessment of potential outcomes due to the unknown reality of the existence of God. 
    * Believing: If God does exist, the rewards are significant; if he doesn't, there's little loss.  Choosing not to believe entails potential loss even if he doesn't exist – punishment in hell. 
* This was summarized in Pascal’s reasoning that choosing for one side or the other of this wager is a choice with high and potentially infinite reward for believing in God. As Pascal saw it, betting on a deity's existence based upon probability would be advantageous; as his argument goes: there will be potential consequences due to uncertainty.

**Pascalian Philosophy:**
* The French philosopher maintained faith as a practical advantage rather than solely on religious authority. He believed that a strong sense of meaning and purpose within the world was achievable through belief, offering a sense of security and order. 
* Pascal’s conclusion implied the most effective means in acquiring genuine belief is not by understanding but through consistent action, similar to the approach in 'Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade', where Indiana ultimately reaches his goal via an actual process rather than simply intellectualization.

**Additional Arguments Against Pascal's Wager:**
* Those opposed claim that this reliance on pragmatic thought diminishes the value of belief systems. The act of pretending or "fake it till you make it" doesn’t necessarily lead to authentic beliefs but merely to a form.  
    * Some individuals who are raised in faiths may end up contradicting their beliefs.

**Kierkegaard's Fideism:**
* Philosopher Soren Kierkegaard offered the idea that religious belief is solely based upon faith, implying that argumentation and evidence were not effective tools for fostering it. 
* This suggests a heightened perspective of spirituality involving mystery and wonder as driving factors in genuine religion.

If you choose not to believe in God and he does exist, you get infinite punishment – hell. Therefore, the smart bet is to put your chips on God existing, every time. Pascal argued that, if there is the slightest chance that God exists—even if that chance is low—only a fool would bet against his existence, given that those stakes are so high. In the face of incomplete information, Pascal decided, we should play the odds, and believe whatever offers us the greatest benefit. It's kind of brilliant, right? But there are a couple of ways you could argue against this.  You might say Pascal's done the math wrong — that choosing to walk the straight and narrow in the service of an imaginary deity actually does cost you something. Like, you might miss out on stuff that you would otherwise want to do, like sleeping in on Sunday mornings, or living a heavy-metal-rock-star lifestyle, or, I dunno, coveting stuff. By this logic, you'd lose out if you abstained from all of that in the name of something that ended up not being real. But Pascal, like William James, disagreed with this line of reasoning, because he saw great personal benefit in being a believer. He thought theists benefited more than non-believers - at least on some level. 
He'd say, It’s just part of what made life meaningful.  And for that reason, he wrote more about belief and the act of faith and not so much from logical arguments to get someone believing.  And there you go.

Ultimately, people believe in things that feel right or true. This isn't always rational or empirical (it's why a lot of us find it difficult to explain what we love - and how, exactly - or at least until a "life moment" gives us a reason—and then it feels 'automatic.' As for Pascal’s thoughts: they had merit. 
He was pragmatic.  In many ways, the pragmatist in him makes sense in a world that demands more than mere philosophy. And what if that's just how we do life and religion and belief?

 Now some critics have pointed out that when it comes to a really usable belief system, you’re going to need something more than ”fake it 'til you make it.”  For example, maybe you were one of those kids raised in a religious household who was never feeling it. We all know people who were immersed in a culture of religious belief from birth and end up later rejecting those beliefs as adults. And for those people trying to force yourself to believe is not only ineffective, it can lead to some pretty serious unhappiness-- the exact opposite of what a pragmatist wants.
So it might be that, for a pragmatist, the best advice for non-believers is just gotta live their lives. Maybe they'll find God and maybe they won't, but making yourself swallow it like medicine doesn’t seem like the way to maximize belief. 

OK, so Pascal said that we should believe in God because belief is just practically useful (this was Soren Kierkegaard who took this concept further — you know Soren Kierkegaard)
And then there’s, FIDEISM which was a whole new school of thought. But let me give some basic ideas: 


* **It's all about faith:** This form of thinking is based on the notion that religious belief can only come from faith alone. In other words,  the "real deal," as Kierkegaard described it—is an inherent quality to belief and something we feel rather than something we can rationally demonstrate through experience. 


Let me give a different example of this: what about science for some people? For example, they might believe science to be the ultimate explanation (and maybe that's good!). 



* **Reason does not matter:**  For Fideists, it’s all about faith; even if facts and logic tell us otherwise. This is an idea that often conflicts with those of our more rational minds (like how does a person decide the value or moral importance of life? Is this something you can measure?). 
* **Life has mystery:**  Kierkegaard said it's important for people to understand faith isn’t something easily solved, and if you try to put logic-driven explanations on the idea, you miss out on what really makes it come alive. It's a mystery all its own—and why should there not be a mystery?
* **Jump for Faith:** Kierkegaard called it “leap of faith," but that means something more than just blindly believing as if nothing else matters. 

So, to make things a little simpler. When you think about Pascal, Kierkegaard…they both felt deeply in their philosophical and historical realities that life is inherently subjective on some level.



To put it simply: The key to the faith-based debate in philosophy lies not just in logic's answer but also how people make sense of something that exists beyond our logical reach like love or religion (which we, too often, have to "prove" through science).

A common argument for belief is formulated around utility. This concept, popularized by French philosopher Blaise Pascal and echoed by 19th-century Danish philosopher Soren Kierkegaard, advocates betting on the existence of God as a practical gamble.  Pascal emphasized that accepting God's existence in face of limited knowledge yields more benefit than enduring potential punishment for disbelief. This reasoning stems from the higher stakes involved.

However, others argue against this approach. Some contend that placing all one's trust in faith is risky. For example, pursuing a religious path might inhibit personal growth and exploration.  Their beliefs, when rooted in action, could be seen as inherently contradictory to Pascal’s pragmatism. 

Kierkegaard pushes the argument further with his concept of "faith" itself. He contends that religion should stem from emotional conviction without relying on logic or arguments, calling it a leap into belief's unfamiliarity. This echoes Indiana Jones’ exploration of religious relics, challenging logic against action-based faith.  He believed true faith rests in irrational leaps of hope. 
 
While philosophical discussions around the practicality of religion remain, this summary highlights key arguments and concepts.

Philosophers have long debated the motivations for true belief.  Some argue that belief is fundamentally about practicality or benefit. This perspective is epitomized by Blaise Pascal's assertion that embracing faith serves as a pathway to attaining spiritual rewards, though his view emphasizes expediency over the intricacies of theological reasoning. The pragmatic approach championed by Pascal suggests convincing oneself through actions and rituals, potentially leading to genuine conviction if followed through consistently. 

Kierkegaard's fideism stands in stark contrast to this pragmatism. He viewed faith's strength lay in its irrationality—a departure from rational thought that necessitates a leap of faith alone to attain understanding. This concept aligns closely with the trials and tribulations faced by Indiana Jones, who navigated perilous situations demanding unwavering faith. 

Though these contrasting viewpoints offer insightful perspectives on the nature of religion, questions arise about the practicality and consequences of relying solely on blind trust or expediency when deciding upon a belief system.  It begs the question: does blind acceptance through emotional manipulation equate to true belief? Can believing in God simply be a means to an end when it doesn't necessarily align with personal values or experiences?

The philosophy of religion is often fraught with contradictions and dilemmas, ranging from questioning whether a specific, tangible deity exists to analyzing the existence of metaphysical entities. Bertrand Russell's teapot thought experiment provides a compelling analogy for this point, wherein its reality remains unprovable while belief in it persists despite lack of evidence. Should a lack of proof automatically equate to legitimacy?

 The notion of "leaping" to something – be it God or an imaginary teapot – raises serious concerns about the potential consequences. One cannot dismiss such "leaping" from tangible grounds with complete impunity, particularly because belief systems have real-world implications for people's lives.  Moreover, if we believe solely on faith, where does that leave us in terms of our reasoning skills?


If a belief system's core is pure trust and the absence of evidence, then anything becomes equally plausible – be it religious beliefs or other subjective matters. What can guide such processes beyond blind faith? One cannot simply accept whatever comes to mind or dismiss potential inconsistencies without thoroughly considering them.
